**On 1 August 2004 one person at one ground station controlled two combat aircraft in flight at once** \[[Boeing X-45][ref_x45_wikipedia]\] \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008]\]. On 3 December the two X-45As, with the call signs Stingray 01 and Stingray 02, flew in coordination under a single pilot-operator for more than an hour \[[Two Boeing X-45A unmanned jets continue coordinated flights][ref_coordinated_flights]\], and in February 2005 they attacked simulated air defences as a team, the ground pilot authorising the first attack \[[Boeing X-45][ref_x45_wikipedia]\]. **That ratio, one to two, is the entire argument of the programme reduced to a number**, and it is the number this article is about.
This is the forty-sixth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the **Two airframes flew sixty-four times between May 2002 and July 2005, and the record of those flights is extensive.** They released a weapon, hit a target, flew in formation, replanned in flight and finally prosecuted a multi-target attack under changing operator priorities \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\]. **The vehicle is documented and its software is not**, so the article dimensions what the software had to deliver rather than describing it.

**The keystone is not aerodynamic and the literature it comes from is not aeronautical.** The quantity that decides whether an unmanned combat aircraft is worth building is the number of vehicles one operator can supervise, and the relation that governs it was written by people studying robots rather than aeroplanes. **At a ratio of one the aeroplane has saved nothing but the pilot's life.** Everything else the concept promises, in crew cost, in persistence and in the willingness to risk the airframe, arrives only when the ratio exceeds one, and the X-45A is where an unmanned combat aircraft was shown to do it.

## The Research Question

**The binding unknown was whether autonomy could raise the number of aircraft one person can supervise above one.**

That question needs stating carefully, because it is easy to state it in a way that is either trivially true or unfalsifiable. **A remotely piloted aircraft has a ratio of one by construction**, since an operator who never looks away has a neglect time of zero and

$$NT = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad FO = \frac{0 + IT}{IT} = 1$$

The pilot has moved from the cockpit to a container and is committed to that airframe for the whole sortie, and what has been bought is that no crew is aboard to be lost. **Those are real and they are not the argument that was being made.** The argument being made was that unmanned aircraft would be cheaper to operate in numbers, and that argument is arithmetic about people.

**The X-45's own programme documents put it in the language of affordability and effectiveness rather than of ratios**, describing a networked system of high performance unmanned air vehicles to prosecute combat missions affordably \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\]. **Affordability in an operational fleet is dominated by people, not by airframes**, and the ratio is the mechanism by which an unmanned aircraft touches that.

**For the second vehicle the question was different and smaller.** The X-45C was to be an operational prototype rather than a demonstrator, and its unknowns were range, payload, carrier compatibility and cost. **It is treated here as the answer to a design question rather than a research one**, and most of the length goes to the X-45A, which is where the research was.

## Programme Origin

**The programme began as a study of whether an unmanned strike aircraft was possible at all.** In the late 1990s the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency began to examine the idea, and in March 1999 Boeing received a contract to build two X-45A technology demonstrators for ground attack, electronic warfare, surveillance and other operations in high-risk airspace \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\].

**The first airframe was completed in September 2000 and did not fly for twenty months.** It arrived at Dryden in November 2000, the second in May 2001, and both underwent extensive ground and taxi testing through 2001 and into 2002 \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\]. **A twenty-month gap between a finished airframe and a first flight is a statement about where the risk was**, and it was not in the airframe.

**The first flight was on 22 May 2002**, lasting fourteen minutes and reaching 195 knots at 7,500 feet \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\] \[[Boeing X-45A Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle begins flight testing, Boeing][ref_boeing_first_flight]\]. The second vehicle followed in November \[[Second Boeing X-45A completes first flight, Boeing][ref_boeing_second_flight]\]. **The sixth flight, in December 2002, was the first on which the aeroplane raised its landing gear**, on a flight of forty minutes at the same speed and altitude \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\], which is a useful measure of how deliberately the envelope was opened.

**The vehicle belongs to a class rather than standing alone** \[[Unmanned combat aerial vehicle][ref_ucav_wikipedia]\], and its immediate ancestor in the unmanned reconnaissance line is the [DarkStar][ref_darkstar_wikipedia] that the [previous article][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] used to calibrate a thrust lapse.

**In parallel the Navy was building its own.** Two contracts for carrier-based demonstrators were awarded in June 2000, to Boeing for the X-46 and to Northrop Grumman for the X-47, both of which are articles still ahead in this series, and in April 2003 the Air Force and Navy efforts were combined into a joint programme that became Joint Unmanned Combat Air Systems, J-UCAS \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\]. **The X-45B and the X-46A were both cancelled before any airframe was built**, and the joint programme's vehicles were the X-45C and the X-47B.

**The programme was funded to continue.** Boeing received 767 million dollars in October 2004 for the J-UCAS capability demonstration \[[Boeing awarded 767 million dollars for the J-UCAS capability demonstration programme][ref_boeing_jucas_award]\], and a full-scale X-45C model was shown at Farnborough that July \[[Boeing X-45C full-scale model makes its debut at Farnborough][ref_boeing_x45c_mockup]\].

**It ended in January 2006.** J-UCAS was cancelled in favour of separate Air Force and Navy programmes, the Air Force turning toward a new manned long-range bomber. The Navy carried the effort forward as a carrier demonstrator competition, and in August 2007 selected the X-47B, terminating the navalised X-45C \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\]. **The reasons were institutional and the article says so rather than inferring a technical failure that the record does not show.**

## Sizing From First Principles

**The demonstrated result is a ratio, and a ratio has a relation behind it.**

### The Quantity That Decides Whether the Aeroplane Pays

**Let the fan-out be the number of vehicles one operator can supervise.** The term and the relation come from human-robot interaction, where the problem of one person and many machines was posed and measured before it was posed for aircraft \[[Olsen and Wood 2004, Fan-out, measuring human control of multiple robots][ref_fanout_acm]\]. **The idea is older than the aircraft application and descends from a literature on teleoperation and process supervision** \[[Sheridan, Telerobotics, automation and human supervisory control][book_sheridan]\].

Let $NT$ be the neglect time, meaning how long a vehicle can be left alone before it needs attention, and $IT$ the interaction time, meaning how long the operator must spend on it once it does. **An operator cycling around a set of identical vehicles can serve them all if and only if the time spent away from any one of them covers the others.** Serving $N$ vehicles takes $N$ interaction times, and each vehicle can wait for at most its neglect time plus the interaction it then receives, so

$$N \, IT \le NT + IT$$

and the largest $N$ satisfying it is the fan-out,

$$FO = \frac{NT + IT}{IT}$$

**Neglect tolerance is measured rather than assumed in that literature**, by putting an operator in a multitasking environment and observing how long each machine survives unattended \[[Crandall et al 2005][research_crandall_goodrich_2005]\], and the measurement framework the field settled on is itself a published object \[[Steinfeld et al 2006][research_steinfeld_fong_2006]\].

**The operator's committed time follows immediately and is the quantity an air force actually buys.**

$$\frac{\text{operator hours}}{\text{vehicle hour}} = \frac{1}{FO} \qquad u = \frac{IT}{NT + IT} = \frac{1}{FO}$$

**The operator's utilisation and the reciprocal of the fan-out are the same number**, which is worth noticing because it says a fully occupied operator is a fan-out of one by definition and no amount of interface work changes that.

**The cost argument the programme was actually making follows from it in one line.** With $C_{a}$ the cost of putting an airframe over the target and $C_{c}$ the crew cost of a manned sortie,

$$C = C_{a} + \frac{C_{c}}{FO}$$

**Only the second term responds to autonomy.** An unmanned aeroplane at a fan-out of one has removed the risk to the crew and none of the crew cost, which is the arithmetic behind the claim that the ratio is the whole argument.

**The relation says something the words do not.** Fan-out is not a property of the operator or of the interface alone. It is a ratio of two times, and **autonomy enters it in exactly one place**, by extending the neglect time. An aeroplane that can be left alone for longer can be one of more.

### Inverting It for the Ratio the X-45A Demonstrated

**One operator and two vehicles bounds the ratio from below, and the relation then bounds the autonomy from below.** An operator who directed two vehicles has shown a fan-out of at least two, so

$$FO = \frac{NT + IT}{IT} \ge 2 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad NT \ge IT$$

**The X-45A could be neglected for at least as long as it took to attend to it.** That is the least autonomy the vehicle can have had, expressed as a ratio, and none of the sources used publishes the ratio in any form. **With a switch cost the same demonstration says more**, since $(NT + IT)/(IT + SC) \ge 2$ gives $NT \ge IT + 2\,SC$, so any time the operator lost in moving between the two vehicles was covered by neglect time as well. **What the demonstration does not bound is the ratio from above.** No source reports one operator attempting three X-45As, so the flights cannot say whether a third could have been supervised, and they give neither time in seconds.

**The same question was being asked of aircraft specifically within three years of the demonstration**, and the answers arrived through operator capacity models rather than through flight tests \[[Cummings et al 2007][research_cummings_nehme_2007]\] \[[Cummings and Mitchell 2008][research_cummings_mitchell_2008]\]. **The scheduling strategy the operator adopts turns out to matter as much as the autonomy does** \[[Cummings and Mitchell 2007][research_cummings_mitchell_2007]\], which is a term the bare relation has no room for.

**It is a modest number and it was a genuine achievement, and both of those are worth saying.** A vehicle that may need attending to as much as half the time is not autonomous in the sense the word is now used. **But the comparison is not with a modern system, it is with a ratio of one**, which is what the armed Predator then in service had, since its ground station crew for one aircraft was a pilot and two sensor operators \[[General Atomics MQ-1 Predator][ref_predator_wikipedia]\].

### What a Higher Ratio Demands

**The relation is unforgiving about what a better ratio costs.** Rearranging,

$$\frac{NT}{IT} = FO - 1$$

| fan-out | required $NT/IT$ | improvement over the X-45A, at most |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | the demonstrated bound |
| 3 | 2 | 2 times |
| 4 | 3 | 3 times |
| 8 | 7 | 7 times |
| 16 | 15 | 15 times |

**The improvement needed is linear in the fan-out and it is measured against a demonstrated ratio of at least one**, so a fleet ratio of eight is not four times harder than the demonstrated two. It is up to seven times harder, and exactly seven times only if the X-45A was flown at its limit, which the record does not show. **The autonomy and the interface have to carry all of it between them**, since the relation has no other term, and the metrics that introduced neglect time state the design goal as reducing interaction effort without diminishing task effectiveness \[[Goodrich and Olsen 2003, Metrics for evaluating human-robot interactions][ref_hri_metrics]\].

**That is the argument for autonomy stated as arithmetic rather than as enthusiasm**, and it also says where the effort has to go. Halving interaction time and doubling neglect time are worth the same amount, and the first is an interface problem while the second is an autonomy problem.

### The Switch Cost, Which the Original Relation Omits

**An operator moving between vehicles pays for the move.** Later work presents a feasibility test for a team that applies when the cost of switching attention between robots or tasks can become prohibitive, and establishes that switch costs can be high and that different tasks impose different ones \[[Goodrich, Quigley and Cosenzo 2005, Task switching and multi-robot teams][ref_task_switching]\]. The form used here adds a switch cost $SC$ to the denominator, since the time spent re-establishing context is time not spent on any vehicle,

$$FO = \frac{NT + IT}{IT + SC}$$

| switch cost | fan-out at $NT = 3\,IT$ |
|---|---|
| 0 | 4.00 |
| 0.25 $IT$ | 3.20 |
| 0.50 $IT$ | 2.67 |
| 1.00 $IT$ | 2.00 |

**A switch cost of half the interaction time removes a third of the fan-out.** At a full interaction time it removes half, taking a system designed for four back to the two the X-45A demonstrated without any change to the vehicle at all. **Interface design is therefore not a detail of this problem, it is one of its two terms**, and the ground station is as much the article under test as the aeroplane.

**The relation also stops describing one operator once there are several**, and the multi-operator case is not the single-operator one multiplied, since operators specialise and hand work to each other \[[Cummings et al 2012][research_cummings_how_2012]\]. **This article stays with the single-operator case because that is what the X-45A demonstrated.**

## The Two Aircraft

**The X-45A and the X-45C are not the same design scaled, although the numbers make them look like it.**

| | X-45A | X-45C |
|---|---|---|
| span | 10.3 m | 14.9 m |
| length | 8.08 m | 11.9 m |
| gross mass | 5,530 kg | 16,600 kg |
| thrust | 28.0 kN | 31.0 kN |
| speed | Mach 0.75 | Mach 0.85 |
| ceiling | 35,000 ft | 40,000 ft |
| mission radius | 497 nm | 1,296 nm |
| internal payload | 680 kg | 2,040 kg |

**The table follows the directory and the sources disagree on the X-45A's design point** \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\]. GlobalSecurity says the X-45A was designed to achieve Mach 0.8 at 40,000 feet with a flight duration of about ninety minutes \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45_globalsecurity]\], against the directory's Mach 0.75 and 35,000 foot ceiling. **Nothing below depends on the X-45A's speed or ceiling.**

**The two aircraft carry the same payload fraction and that is the fact the rest of the table follows from.**

$$\frac{m_{\text{payload}}}{m_{\text{gross}}} = \frac{680}{5{,}530} = 0.12297 \qquad \frac{2{,}040}{16{,}600} = 0.12289$$

**They agree to four significant figures, and their ratio is 0.99940.** Nothing in the sources says this was intended and the arithmetic says it happened.

**The mass then scales as very nearly the cube of the span, which looks like geometric similarity and is not.**

$$m \propto b^{\,n} \qquad n = \frac{\ln \left( m_{2} / m_{1} \right)}{\ln \left( b_{2} / b_{1} \right)} = \frac{\ln \left( 16{,}600 / 5{,}530 \right)}{\ln \left( 14.9 / 10.3 \right)} = 2.977$$

**The same exponent computed from the payloads instead of the masses gives 2.976**, which is the same number, and that is the explanation.

$$\frac{\ln \left( 2{,}040 / 680 \right)}{\ln \left( 14.9 / 10.3 \right)} = 2.976 \qquad \frac{m_{\text{payload},2}}{m_{\text{payload},1}} = 3.0000$$

**The payload was tripled exactly, the payload fraction was held, and the gross mass therefore tripled too.** The span then followed from the mass rather than the mass from the span.

**It is not geometry and it is not a coincidence either.** The [X-37][related_post_a334_boeing_x37] measured 1.924 against the Shuttle orbiter and the [X-38][related_post_a335_scaled_composites_x38] measured 3.507 against the X-24A, and in both cases the exponent said something about the design. **Here the X-45C's wing planform was changed to the naval one and the two aircraft are not geometrically similar in any other respect**, so an exponent of three is a fact about a held payload fraction and not about a shape. **A scaling exponent that arrives from the mission rather than from the geometry looks identical in the arithmetic and means something entirely different**, which is the warning this series has recorded before against reading an exponent as a property of the technology.

**What is not similar at all is the performance.**

$$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{T_{\text{SL}}}{m \, g} \qquad \left. \frac{T}{W} \right|_{\text{X-45A}} = \frac{28{,}000}{5{,}530 \times 9.80665} = 0.516 \qquad \left. \frac{T}{W} \right|_{\text{X-45C}} = 0.190$$

**A factor of 2.71.** The X-45C is three times the mass on ten percent more thrust, because it is an operational aeroplane carrying three times the payload two and a half times as far, and the demonstrator was a lightly loaded airframe on a proportionally large engine. **Geometrically similar in mass and nothing like each other in the air.**

### A Thrust Figure That Looks Wrong and Is Not

**The X-45C's quoted thrust looks wrong.** The engine is given as a General Electric F404 variant at 7,000 pounds force \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\] \[[X-45C, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45c_globalsecurity]\], and the F404 family's dry rating is nearer 11,000 with an augmented rating of 17,700 \[[General Electric F404][ref_f404_wikipedia]\]. **The X-45A's own engine is a Honeywell F124 of 28 kilonewtons** \[[Honeywell and ITEC F124][ref_f124_wikipedia]\], which is a non-augmented turbofan of the class used in trainers and light attack aircraft. **Parsch himself warns that his figures may be inaccurate**, since the data given by several sources show slight variations \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\].

**The test available is whether the low figure can hold the vehicle's own stated ceiling.** At the ceiling the thrust available equals the drag, so

$$T_{\text{avail}}(h, M) = \frac{W}{L/D} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \frac{L}{D} = \frac{W}{T_{\text{avail}}}$$

with the installed thrust following the corrected mass flow of a fixed engine, which is the standard corrected-parameter machinery of engine performance \[[Mattingly, Aircraft engine design][book_mattingly_engine_design]\] \[[Cumpsty, Jet propulsion][book_cumpsty]\],

$$T_{\text{avail}} = T_{\text{SL}} \, \frac{p}{p_{\text{SL}}} \, \frac{\left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3.5}}{\sqrt{\left( T / T_{\text{SL}} \right) \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)}}$$

At 40,000 feet and Mach 0.85 the weight is 162.8 kilonewtons and the three candidate ratings give

| sea-level rating | available at the ceiling | lift to drag ratio it demands |
|---|---|---|
| 7,000 lbf as published | 9,964 N | 16.3 |
| 11,000 lbf, the dry class | 15,658 N | 10.4 |
| 17,700 lbf, augmented | 25,195 N | 6.5 |

**A clean subsonic flying wing of this size reaches sixteen to eighteen** \[[Torenbeek, Synthesis of subsonic airplane design][book_torenbeek]\] \[[Filippone, Advanced aircraft flight performance][book_filippone]\] \[[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]\], **so the published figure is admissible and the suspicion does not survive.** What the check produces instead is better than the error would have been, because **it pins a quantity no source publishes.** The X-45C must have achieved a lift to drag ratio of at least 16.3 to do what its own specification says it does.

**The demand of 16.3 is near the top of that range and the configuration is the reason to take the top seriously rather than the middle.** A tailless aeroplane trims without a tail, so its efficiency and its static stability are set together rather than separately, and the literature treats that coupling as the configuration's defining aerodynamic question \[[Kashiwagura and Shimoyama 2018][research_kashiwagura_shimoyama_2018]\]. **Drag reduction on such an aeroplane is pursued through the same surfaces that trim it** \[[Cusher and Gopalarathnam 2012][research_cusher_gopalarathnam_2012]\], which is why a clean flying wing can reach a ratio a conventional aeroplane of the same size would not and why the figure is sensitive to how the aeroplane is trimmed. **This supports the admissibility of the published thrust and it does not establish the ratio**, which remains a lower bound derived from the vehicle's own stated ceiling.

**The bound is not an artefact of the exact ceiling.**

| assumed ceiling | assumed Mach | required lift to drag |
|---|---|---|
| 35,000 ft | 0.85 | 12.9 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.80 | 17.1 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.85 | 16.3 |
| 40,000 ft | 0.90 | 15.6 |
| 45,000 ft | 0.85 | 20.8 |

**The 40,000 foot rows are all admissible and the 45,000 foot row is not**, since 20.8 lies above the sixteen to eighteen that the sources cited above give for a clean subsonic flying wing of this size. **The thrust figure and the ceiling figure therefore pin each other**, and the pair is self-consistent at exactly the ceiling the sources quote. **Two figures that corroborate is a weaker result than an error would have been and a truer one.**

## Dependent Systems

### The Configuration, and the Question the Previous Article Left Open

**The X-45A is tailless, with trailing-edge elevons and a yaw thrust vectoring nozzle, and has no vertical surfaces.** In the absence of vertical surfaces yaw was controlled by thrust vectoring \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\] together with oppositely deflected outboard elevons, in what NASA's account of the design calls a crow mix \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008_b]\], and the flight controls are all-electric except for the nose wheel steering and the brakes \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45_globalsecurity]\]. **The absence of a fin is a signature decision before it is an aerodynamic one** \[[Knott, Shaeffer and Tuley, Radar cross section][book_knott]\], and the configuration has a documented history far older than the jet age \[[Wooldridge, Winged wonders, the story of the flying wings][book_wooldridge]\]. **The stability the fin would have supplied is replaced by feedback** \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin_reid]\] \[[Nelson, Flight stability and automatic control][book_nelson]\] \[[Anderson, Fundamentals of aerodynamics][book_anderson]\].

**That is close to the configuration the [previous article in this series][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] derived could not meet an operational crosswind landing requirement.** It found that the required vector angle for a crosswind of fixed speed depends on Mach number alone, that at equal throttle the approach is the easiest case in the envelope, and that the approach binds anyway because the throttle is nearly closed. **And then the X-45A landed sixty-four times.**

**The two results are compatible and the arithmetic says why.** The demand goes as the dynamic pressure times the sideslip a fixed crosswind produces, and the authority goes as the thrust the approach leaves available. **Neither the wing area nor the yaw derivative is published for the X-45A**, so the comparison is made against the F-22 case the previous article computed, in which the airframe terms appear in both and the throttle does not.

**The thrust an approach requires is the one relation in this comparison that does not involve the wing at all.** On a glide slope $\gamma$ at a lift to drag ratio $L/D$,

$$\frac{T}{W} = \frac{1}{L/D} - \sin \gamma \qquad \Pi = \frac{W}{T_{\text{SL}}} \left( \frac{1}{L/D} - \sin \gamma \right)$$

which for the X-45A at a landing lift to drag ratio of nine on three degrees gives $\Pi = 0.114$. **The approach speed and the sideslip a crosswind produces do involve the wing**, through

$$V_{\text{app}} = 1.3 \sqrt{\frac{2 m g}{\rho \, S \, C_{L,\max}}} \qquad S = \frac{b^{2}}{A\!R} \qquad \beta = \arctan \frac{V_{c}}{V_{\text{app}}}$$

and the demand the vectoring must meet is the product of the dynamic pressure and that angle,

$$D \equiv q \, \beta = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V_{\text{app}}^{2} \arctan \frac{V_{c}}{V_{\text{app}}}$$

**The comparison is then a ratio of ratios, in which the airframe constants of the previous article's case appear in both halves and cancel.**

$$\text{margin} = \frac{\Pi / \Pi_{\text{F-22}}}{D / D_{\text{F-22}}}$$

| | X-45A | F-22, from the previous article |
|---|---|---|
| approach thrust fraction | 11.4 percent | 7.2 percent |
| sideslip in a 15 m/s crosswind | 10.1 deg | 11.0 deg |
| demand index, relative | 1.09 | 1 |
| available thrust, relative | 1.58 | 1 |
| **net margin, relative** | **1.45** | **1** |

**The X-45A is better off by a factor of 1.45 and the reason is the throttle.** It is a light aeroplane on a proportionally large engine, so the thrust that a three degree approach requires is a larger share of what the engine can produce, and the vectoring authority scales with that share.

**The wing area is not published and it does real work, so the conclusion is tested across the plausible range.**

| aspect ratio | wing area | wing loading | approach speed | net margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | 35.4 m² | 156 kg/m² | 121 kn | 1.98 |
| 4.0 | 26.5 m² | 209 kg/m² | 139 kn | 1.71 |
| 5.5 | 19.3 m² | 287 kg/m² | 163 kn | 1.45 |
| 7.0 | 15.2 m² | 365 kg/m² | 184 kn | 1.28 |

**Every row leaves the X-45A better off than the F-22, so the conclusion does not depend on the assumed wing.** The thrust fraction does not move at all across that table, because it follows from the glide slope and the lift to drag ratio rather than from the wing, and only the demand column responds.

**The rest of the reconciliation is the previous article's own caveat and not a new argument.** That article said explicitly that a vehicle landing into wind on a long runway at a test range faces a much weaker requirement than an operational fighter does. **The X-45A is exactly that vehicle**, flying at Edwards with the option of waiting for the wind. **So the earlier conclusion survives, the X-45A is not a counterexample to it, and the margin by which it is not a counterexample has been computed rather than asserted.**

**The vectoring-only model also understates the X-45A's yaw authority.** NASA's account of the design records that oppositely deflected outboard elevons were used for yaw stability and control alongside the nozzle \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008_b]\], which the previous article's model of a thrust-vectored tailless aeroplane does not include. **No source gives the authority those surfaces add**, so they strengthen the conclusion without changing the computed margin.

### The Weapons Bay

**An internal bay is a hole in a low observable aeroplane, and opening it is the moment the aeroplane stops being one.** The X-45A carried a bay of 680 kilograms capacity, explicitly to test all phases of weapons handling and deployment \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\], and the X-45C was to carry 2,040 kilograms, being two GBU-31 Joint Direct Attack Munitions \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\].

**In March 2004 the X-45A released a weapon for the first time** \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\], **and in April it hit a target with an inert satellite-guided bomb** \[[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]\]. **The autonomy claim in that milestone is narrower than it is usually reported.** The operator gave three commands, being target confirmation, arm and release consent, and the aircraft then performed the manoeuvres, the bay door operations and the release sequence autonomously under human supervision, dropping a 250-pound Small Smart Bomb from its internal bay at 35,000 feet and Mach 0.67 \[[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]\]. The release was autonomous in the sense that the aeroplane executed it without a pilot flying the aeroplane, and the decision to attack that target was made by a person. **The distinction matters and is kept throughout**, because the later milestones moved the line and the record says where.

### The Link, and What It Is For

**A supervised aeroplane needs a link, and the link's properties set the interaction time in the fan-out relation directly.** A high-latency or low-bandwidth link raises the time an operator needs to understand a situation and to act, which lowers the fan-out for a fixed autonomy.

**The coupling is not qualitative and writing it down says exactly what a latency figure would be worth.** A round trip of $\tau$ each way is added to every interaction, so

$$IT = IT_{0} + 2\tau \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad FO = \frac{NT + IT_{0} + 2\tau}{IT_{0} + 2\tau + SC}$$

**Latency appears in the numerator and the denominator and does not cancel**, because it lengthens the interaction without lengthening the neglect.

**That effect was measured in 1963, thirty-nine years before this aeroplane flew.** Sheridan and Ferrell put a transmission delay into a remote manipulation task and found the operator's completion time growing with it in a way practice did not remove \[[Sheridan and Ferrell 1963][research_sheridan_ferrell_1963]\], and four years later the same authors named the response to it, which was to stop transmitting movements and start transmitting intentions \[[Ferrell and Sheridan 1967][research_ferrell_sheridan_1967]\]. **Supervisory control was invented as an answer to latency**, and the X-45A is an aeroplane built on that answer. Taking a ten second interaction and a neglect time three times it,

| one-way latency | fan-out | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 0 s | 4.00 | none |
| 0.25 s | 3.86 | 3.6 percent |
| 0.5 s | 3.73 | 6.8 percent |
| 1 s | 3.50 | 12.5 percent |
| 2 s | 3.14 | 21.4 percent |

**A satellite round trip costs a fifth of the fan-out on those assumptions**, and a line-of-sight link costs almost nothing. **That is a design consequence rather than an observation**, and it is the reason a supervised combat aircraft wants its operator within line of sight or its autonomy raised to compensate.

**This is the sharpest coupling in the article and the public record does not quantify it for this aeroplane.** NASA's review of the test site shows ultra high frequency, L-band and fighter data link command and control channels and L-band telemetry for the demonstration \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008]\], and none of the sources this article uses gives a latency figure, a bandwidth figure or a link budget for any of them. **The relation says what such a figure would buy and nothing here can say what it was**, which is recorded rather than filled with an assumption.

### Structure and Affordability

**No source this article uses describes the X-45A's structure.** Affordability was a stated programme objective rather than a consequence, and the flight control paper states the programme's aim as exploiting the freedom of relocating the pilot outside the vehicle to enable a new paradigm in aircraft affordability \[[Davidson 2004][research_davidson_2004]\]. GlobalSecurity puts the X-45 unmanned combat air vehicle at 10 to 15 million dollars apiece, about a third of the 45 million dollars it gives for the Joint Strike Fighter \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, GlobalSecurity][ref_x45_globalsecurity]\], which is a projection for an operational aircraft and not a cost of the demonstrator. **No cost figure for the demonstrator airframe is among the sources used**, so the objective is recorded and not evaluated.

## The Flight Test Record

**Sixty-four flights over thirty-eight months.**

$$\dot{n} = \frac{64}{38} = 1.68 \ \text{flights per month}$$

**That rate is a statement about what was under test.** The record runs in software blocks \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\], and a T-33 carried the vehicle's management system computers in flight before the X-45A first flew, and the arrangement allowed each mission to be rehearsed on it to validate the mission plan and train the team \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\], serving for software checkout and mission planning verification \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008]\]. **A programme that flew more often would have been testing something else.**

The record, as the directory \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\] and NASA \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\] give it, runs in software blocks rather than in envelope points.

| date | milestone |
|---|---|
| May 2002 | first flight, 14 minutes, 195 kn at 7,500 ft |
| November 2002 | second vehicle flies |
| December 2002 | landing gear raised in flight for the first time |
| February 2003 | Block 1 complete, being taxi, takeoff, landing, navigation and basic communication |
| November 2003 | Block 2 testing begins, including communication with manned aircraft |
| March 2004 | first weapon released |
| April 2004 | target hit with an inert satellite-guided bomb |
| August 2004 | two vehicles in coordinated flight under one operator |
| October 2004 | Block 3 begins, including in-flight mission replanning |
| July 2005 | programme complete after 64 flights |

**The final mission is the one worth quoting in full, because it is where the ratio was actually earned.** It included detecting and avoiding multiple simulated threats, determining which of several possible targets to attack, replanning after the operator changed target priorities, and conducting the attacks with one or two aircraft \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\].

**Read against the fan-out relation, every clause of that sentence is an attempt to raise neglect time.** Detecting and avoiding threats without asking is neglect time. Choosing among targets is neglect time. **Replanning after the operator changed priorities is the opposite**, being an interaction, and it is the one clause that describes the operator doing something. **The mission was designed so that the operator's contribution was a priority change and not a control input**, which is what supervision means.

**Both airframes survived and both are in museums**, one at the National Museum of the United States Air Force \[[Boeing X-45A J-UCAS, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x45a_museum]\] and one in the Military Unmanned Aerial Vehicles exhibit at the National Air and Space Museum \[[Military Unmanned Aerial Vehicles exhibit, National Air and Space Museum][ref_smithsonian_uav]\]. **No airframe was lost**, and NASA records the sixty-four research flights as safe and successful \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008_b]\].

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**The sources this article uses hold no numerical pair of a ground prediction and a flight result for this aeroplane, and that absence is the first finding.** They include no test report, flight log or software specification for the X-45A. The seven research papers whose titles name the aeroplane are where such a pair would be sought, as the section headed The Source Base records, and the abstracts of four of them and the full text of a fifth describe the testing without giving its numbers. **The aeroservoelastic paper records the one ground prediction these sources show being revised by test before flight.** Its flight control filters were first designed from structural and aerodynamic models, initial structural mode interaction testing prompted a post-test investigation of both the models and the analysis, and the filters were redesigned from the improved models before the flight results it summarises \[[Reichenbach 2003][research_reichenbach_2003]\]. The flight control paper reports flight test results for the system that controlled the vehicle through taxi, takeoff, flight and landing during envelope expansion \[[Davidson 2004][research_davidson_2004]\], the formation paper presents flight results for the guidance behind formation taxi and flight \[[Brinker and Barker 2005][research_brinker_barker_2005]\], and the first flight paper summarises the test accomplishments up to and including the first flight \[[Wise 2003][research_wise_2003]\]. NASA's account of the design records that the shape passed through computational fluid dynamics analysis, design refinement and wind tunnel testing before the flight article was built \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008_b]\], and gives no figures either. The first flight on 22 May 2002 lasted fourteen minutes and reached 195 knots at 7,500 feet \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\] \[[Boeing X-45A Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle begins flight testing, Boeing][ref_boeing_first_flight]\], and it can be reported but not compared with a stated prediction.

**What the record does show is where the prediction was done, and it was done on the ground at length.** Both airframes underwent extensive ground and taxi testing through 2001 and into 2002 \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\], and autonomous ground taxi was demonstrated on 24 October 2001 \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008]\]. Dryden engineers designed the ground control laws for taxi, takeoff and landing relying heavily on simulation models, and ran ground vibration tests to update the analytical models and calculate the flutter margins \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\], exciting the airframe with three 50 pound shakers and measuring it with 176 accelerometers \[[Cosentino 2008][research_cosentinogaryb_2008]\]. The landing gear was not raised in flight until the sixth flight, and the T-33 surrogate allowed each mission to be rehearsed first \[[X-45 Unmanned Combat Air Vehicle, NASA][ref_x45_nasa]\]. The inert satellite-guided bomb that hit its target in April 2004 \[[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]\] is the flight result that any ground separation analysis would be judged against. **No such analysis is among the sources used**, so the hit confirms that whatever prediction was made was adequate and says nothing about the margin by which it was.

**The one prediction this article can set against a flight result is an analytical one from outside the programme.** The [previous article][related_post_a341_x44_two_aircraft] in this series derived that a tailless aeroplane yawed by thrust vectoring could not meet an operational crosswind landing requirement, and the X-45A then landed sixty-four times in a tailless configuration yawed in part by thrust vectoring. **The two are compatible and the reconciliation is argued in the section headed Dependent Systems**, where an approach thrust fraction of 11.4 percent against 7.2 percent for the F-22 case leaves the X-45A better off by a factor between 1.28 and 1.98 across the plausible wing, and where the test range's option of waiting for the wind carries the rest. **That comparison sets a prediction beside a flight count and not beside flight data**, since no crosswind, sideslip or nozzle deflection from any X-45A landing has been published.

**The keystone result reverses the usual direction of comparison.** The fan-out relation was posed and measured in human-robot interaction before it was posed for aircraft. The metrics that founded it measure a robot's autonomy by its neglect time and the attention it demands by free time and fan-out \[[Goodrich and Olsen 2003, Metrics for evaluating human-robot interactions][ref_hri_metrics]\], principles of efficient interaction were compiled from evaluations of neglect tolerance and interface efficiency \[[Goodrich and Olsen][research_goodrich_olsen]\], and the fan-out equation was then defined and validated experimentally \[[Olsen and Wood 2004, Fan-out, measuring human control of multiple robots][ref_fanout_acm]\]. No ground estimate of the X-45A's own neglect time or interaction time is among the sources used for the flight to confirm. The flight returned the ratio, one operator to two vehicles first in August 2004 \[[Boeing X-45][ref_x45_wikipedia]\] and for more than an hour in December \[[Two Boeing X-45A unmanned jets continue coordinated flights][ref_coordinated_flights]\], and the section headed Sizing From First Principles works backward from that ratio to a neglect time at least equal to the interaction time. **Here the flight is the measurement and the relation supplies the inference**, and the operator capacity models that took up the question for aircraft arrived after the demonstration rather than before it \[[Cummings et al 2007][research_cummings_nehme_2007]\].

**For the X-45C the comparison is empty, because the aeroplane never flew.** Its specification gave a ceiling of 40,000 feet on an engine rated at 7,000 pounds force, and the section headed The Two Aircraft shows that the pair is self-consistent only if the aeroplane reaches a lift to drag ratio of at least 16.3. **That bound is a prediction derived from a specification, and flight never returned a number to set beside it.**

## What the Data Changed

**The X-45A settled that the ratio can exceed one, and nothing since has settled how far.**

**Whether the demonstrated fan-out of two has since been exceeded for armed aircraft in operational service is not settled by the sources this article uses**, and the article assumes neither answer. The armed aircraft in service when the X-45A flew was crewed on the ground by a pilot and two sensor operators for each aircraft \[[General Atomics MQ-1 Predator][ref_predator_wikipedia]\], which is a ratio of one.

**The configuration propagated and the programme did not.** The tailless low observable planform with internal carriage is what the X-47B flew from a carrier and what has appeared repeatedly since \[[Northrop Grumman X-47B][ref_x47b_wikipedia]\]. **J-UCAS itself was cancelled in January 2006 before either competitor's vehicle had flown**, in favour of separate service programmes and, for the Air Force, a manned bomber \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\]. Flight testing of both systems had been expected to begin in 2007 \[[Parsch, Boeing X-45 and X-46, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x45]\], a Boeing release of April 2004 scheduled the first X-45C flight for mid-2006 \[[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]\] and one of December 2004 for early 2007 \[[Two Boeing X-45A unmanned jets continue coordinated flights][ref_coordinated_flights]\], and the X-45C never flew. The X-47B first flew on 4 February 2011 \[[Northrop Grumman X-47B][ref_x47b_wikipedia]\].

**The clearest thing the programme changed is what a demonstrator is expected to demonstrate.** The X-45A's milestones are software blocks and not envelope points. **The aeroplane was the test rig and the flight control laws were the fixture.**

**That shape is now the normal one and the test community says so in its own words.** The operational test lessons drawn from unmanned aircraft while the X-45A was flying already treat the system and not the airframe as the article under test \[[Carr et al 2003][research_carr_lambrecht_2003]\], and a decade later the problem had been named as a standing challenge for test and evaluation and not as a property of any one programme \[[Clark et al 2014][research_clark_kearns_2014]\] \[[Yeh 2018][research_yeh_2018]\]. **What makes an autonomous aircraft hard to test is that its behaviour is a function of a situation and not of a flight condition**, so an envelope point does not bound it and a block of software has to be argued about instead.

**The survey below maps the field these vehicles sit in and is kept separate from the curated sources that carry the argument.** Every record comes from Crossref or from the Technical Reports Server of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, is admitted under the subject rule stated in the section headed The Source Base, and is assigned to exactly one cluster.

**The survey draws on two literatures and not one.** The keystone relation comes from human-robot interaction, where the papers carry no aeronautical vocabulary whatever, so a survey admitting only the vocabulary of aircraft would contain none of them.

### What the Shape of the Survey Says

**The autonomy clusters together outweigh the aerodynamic ones and that is the correct shape for this subject.** Autonomy and mission management, multi-vehicle coordination, human supervisory control, and verification of autonomous software hold 3,095 records between them, against 230 for the aerodynamics of the configuration. **An aeroplane whose risk sat in its software has a literature whose mass sits there too.**

**The median publication year is 2015 and 50.8 percent of dated records are from 2015 or later.** The subject did not stop when the programme did. **It moved to a different community**, and the recent weight is in autonomy and cooperative control, where records from 2015 or later make up 64.5 percent of the cluster on autonomy and 67.3 percent of the cluster on multi-vehicle coordination, against 35.8 percent for the aerodynamics of the configuration.

**One thousand and two records predate 2000 and they are not decoration.** Supervisory control was posed as a problem of remote manipulation in the 1960s, long before an aeroplane needed it \[[Sheridan and Ferrell 1963][research_sheridan_ferrell_1963]\] \[[Ferrell and Sheridan 1967][research_ferrell_sheridan_1967]\], and the relation this article rests on is a descendant of that work.

**The datalink cluster holds 87 records, fewer than all but two others, and the smallness looks real rather than an artefact.** The likeliest reason is that military link performance seldom reaches the open bibliographic record, and only fifteen research titles in the whole survey pair a latency or a delay with an unmanned aircraft, as the section headed The Source Base counts. **That is a limit on the survey and not a gap in the field**, and it is the one place where this article's coupling between the link and the fan-out cannot be supported from the literature.

**The survey can also be read against this article's conclusions instead of its topics, and that is a different question.** A conclusion is not a topic, and a survey assembled around a subject can be silent on the thing the subject was used to argue.

**The survey supports the aeronautical conclusions unevenly.** The crosswind comparison inherited from the X-44 article rests on 245 records on yaw control without a fin, and the flight test methodology behind the claim about software blocks on 58. **The lift to drag ratio that the thrust figure pins rests on only twenty-nine**, because most published work on that ratio concerns airfoil sections, induced drag theory and configurations other than the flying wing, which the subject rule excludes, and the range of sixteen to eighteen that the bound is tested against is sourced to textbooks. **The conclusions about supervision sit on between eleven and thirty-two records each, fewer than either well-served aeronautical conclusion**, and the reason is worth stating. The question of how many vehicles one operator can hold is named by phrases that also name a much larger literature about photogrammetry, path planning and crop estimation. **The vocabulary does not discriminate**, which is a different condition from a subject being unstudied, and no choice of search terms repairs it.

**The sharpest instance sits underneath this article's most exposed claim.** The assertion that a ratio of two has not been beaten in twenty years is a statement about reported operator to vehicle ratios, and the survey holds eleven records that use that vocabulary. **Four of the eleven are a different subject wearing the same words**, being the organisational span of control that asks how many subordinates a commander may hold, which is the ancestor of this article's question and not an instance of it. **They are kept and not removed**, because the lineage is real and a reader is better served by seeing it named than by finding the cluster quietly smaller.

### Human supervisory control and the span of control

**This is the cluster the article's keystone comes from, and most of it is not an aeronautical literature.** It holds human-robot interaction, the fan-out relation and its successors, neglect time and interaction time, operator workload and situation awareness, levels of automation, trust in automation and the out-of-the-loop problem, together with teleoperation under transmission delay, which is where the latency term in the section headed Dependent Systems comes from. **Of its 1,394 records, 315 name an aircraft, a drone, a helicopter, an aerial or uninhabited vehicle, aviation, flight, a pilot, a cockpit, air traffic or airspace in their titles**, so a survey admitting only the vocabulary of aircraft would miss more than three-quarters of it, which is why this survey admits the vocabulary of supervising a machine as a second route onto the subject.

### Autonomy, mission management and onboard decision making

**What the X-45A's software blocks were actually delivering.** Mission management architectures, onboard replanning, contingency handling, deliberative and reactive planning, and the long argument about what autonomy means when the word is used as a selling point. **The programme's milestones were all software milestones after the first year**, and this is the field those milestones were drawn from.

### Multi-vehicle coordination and cooperative control

**The other half of the fan-out problem, approached from the machine's side.** Cooperative control, task allocation, consensus, distributed decision making, formation flight and swarm coordination. **Autonomy raises the fan-out by raising neglect time**, and this cluster is where the algorithms that do so live. **Eighteen records sit here because particle swarm optimisation shares the word swarm**, and they are kept because their subjects, most of them path planning, are on this article's subject.

### Tailless configurations and their control effectors

**The configuration, and the thread this article inherits from its predecessor.** Tailless and flying wing aerodynamics, elevons, split drag rudders, control allocation among redundant effectors, and yaw by thrust vectoring. **The X-45A flew the configuration the previous article in this series analysed and found wanting for an operational fighter**, and it flew it sixty-four times.

### Flight control law design and handling qualities

**What replaces the pilot's hands.** Control law design, stability augmentation, gain scheduling, adaptive and robust control, and the handling qualities framework that an unmanned aeroplane inherits without inheriting the pilot who defined it. **A handling quality is a statement about a human being**, and this cluster is where the field works out what the term means when there is nobody aboard. **Of its 472 records, 232 concern unmanned aircraft by their titles**, and none of those names a rotorcraft or a vertical takeoff type.

**The discipline the section headed The Two Aircraft borrows its arithmetic from.** Conceptual design, initial sizing, mass and weight estimation, payload fractions and the sizing loop, for combat, military and unmanned aircraft, for blended wing body designs of any class, and as general methods. **A mass exponent near three that arrives from a held payload fraction is the kind of result this literature exists to explain**, and the section headed The Source Base records how thinly the survey treats scaling across size itself.

**The engine and what the airframe does to it.** Turbofan cycle and installed performance, embedded inlet integration, pressure recovery and specific fuel consumption. **The article uses this literature for one purpose**, being to test whether a published thrust figure can hold a published ceiling.

### Unmanned combat aircraft and the strike mission

**The vehicle class, as distinct from the far larger literature on unmanned aircraft in general.** Armed unmanned aircraft, strike mission analysis and the operational arguments for and against them. **This cluster is deliberately narrow**, because the civil small aircraft literature now dwarfs the combat one and would otherwise swamp the survey. **Four records in this cluster name the X-45A in their titles**, on its first flight, its aeroservoelastic design and test, its flight control design and test, and the formation taxi and flight of the two vehicles.

### Aerodynamics of the configuration

**The flow the vehicle lives in.** Lift, drag and the lift to drag ratio of tailless, flying wing, blended wing body and delta planforms and of combat and unmanned aircraft, their vortex flows, the cruise, range, ceiling and takeoff performance of fixed-wing aircraft, lateral-directional and crosswind behaviour, and the wind tunnel and flight techniques that correlate prediction with flight. **The X-45's aerodynamic record is thin because the aerodynamics were not the point**, the configuration having been chosen for signature and the programme's risk having sat in the software, and one record in this cluster names the X-45 planform.

### Suppression of enemy air defences and time-critical targeting

**The mission the vehicle was built for and the one that sets its clock.** Suppression of enemy air defences, emitter location, time-critical targeting, the kill chain, threat evaluation and jamming. **A mobile emitter that shuts down sets a deadline**, and whether the loop closes inside it is the question the mission poses to the autonomy.

### Internal weapons carriage and store separation

**A bay is a hole in a low observable aeroplane and opening it is the moment it stops being one.** Internal carriage, store separation, cavity flow and acoustics, and guided weapon delivery accuracy. **The X-45A released a weapon from an internal bay in 2004, the release sequence performed autonomously under human supervision** \[[Boeing unmanned combat aircraft makes aviation history][ref_aviation_history]\], and no ground separation analysis for it is among the sources used.

### Programme, acquisition and the cost of a demonstrator

**Why the programme ended, which is the part of this story that is documented.** Acquisition, cost estimation, technology readiness and the transition from demonstrator to programme of record. **J-UCAS was cancelled in January 2006 and the reasons were institutional rather than technical**, and the cluster holds one review of the flight test site processes and personnel of the X-45A demonstration programme.
